papers.title: CsBPC6-CsNACX2-CsTCS1 Module Positively Regulates Caffeine Biosynthesis Under PEG-Induced Drought Stress in Tea Plants (Camellia sinensis).
papers.abstractText: Caffeine biosynthesis in tea plants (Camellia sinensis) is dynamically regulated by environmental cues; however, the mechanisms linking early drought signals to caffeine accumulation remain unclear. Here, we show that acute PEG-induced osmotic stress induces rapid caffeine accumulation, accompanied by transcriptional activation of the key biosynthetic gene CsTCS1. Through integrative analyses, including GWAS and co-expression network modeling, we identified a CsBPC6-CsNACX2-CsTCS1 module as a central regulatory hub. Mechanistically, CsNACX2 directly binds the promoter of the caffeine synthase gene CsTCS1, activating its transcription and promoting caffeine accumulation. Moreover, the drought-responsive transcription factor CsBPC6 acts upstream to transactivate CsNACX2. Functional validation using gene silencing and transient overexpression assays confirmed that the CsBPC6-CsNACX2-CsTCS1 module positively regulates caffeine biosynthesis under PEG-induced drought conditions. Collectively, our findings uncover a previously uncharacterized drought-responsive transcriptional module governing caffeine biosynthesis, providing new mechanistic insights into how environmental cues regulate secondary metabolism in tea plants.

papers.title: Identification of potential regulators of caffeine biosynthesis in shading- and nano‐selenium-treated tea leaves based on integrated bioinformatics and AlphaFold3 analysis.
papers.abstractText: Caffeine is an important flavor and bioactive compound in tea, yet external stimuli-induced regulatory networks of caffeine biosynthesis remain largely unclear. Our study showed that shading and nano‐selenium (SeNPs) treatments respectively increased caffeine content in tea leaves from 35.96 mg/g to approximately 43 mg/g, whereas their combined treatment exerted a synergistic effect, raising it to 51.12 mg/g. Correlation of transcriptome with caffeine content and treatment factors via WGCNA and Mantel tests identified 4 key gene modules and 64 transcription factors (TFs). To accelerate TF screening, we established a rapid and high-throughput screening strategy by integrating AlphaFold3 with JASPAR motif prediction, resulting in 10 candidate TF-DNA complexes. Subsequent validation in yeast and tobacco systems confirmed that CsTSO1 directly binds to the promoter of CsSAMS. Our study uncovers how shading and SeNPs modulate caffeine biosynthesis in tea plants, and provide an AI-assisted framework for efficient TF screening in plant metabolic network.

papers.title: Effect of coffee lyophilizate addition on the physicochemical properties and bioactive profile of yogurt during storage.
papers.abstractText: This study investigated the effect of caffeinated Arabica and decaffeinated coffee lyophilizate (0.6 g/100 g), incorporated either before or after fermentation, on the phenolic compound profile, caffeine and diterpene content, antioxidant activity, and physicochemical properties of yogurt during 20 d of refrigerated storage. Yogurts were produced from commercially available pasteurized and homogenized cow's milk (2.0% fat) using a thermophilic starter culture comprising Streptococcus thermophilus, Lactobacillus acidophilus, and Bifidobacterium animalis ssp. lactis (Lyofast SAB 440B). Total phenolic losses during lyophilization amounted to 14.0% and 19.0% for caffeinated and decaffeinated preparations, respectively, with feruloylquinic acid isomers showing the highest susceptibility to degradation (losses of 55-72%). Coffee enrichment resulted in an approximately 9-10-fold increase in total phenolic content relative to control yogurt, with overall phenolic retention reaching 73-85% of theoretical values. After-fermentation addition yielded higher extractable phenolic content, while before-fermentation addition was associated with lower extractable phenolics but superior hydroxyl radical scavenging capacity (OHSC), potentially reflecting the formation of polyphenol-protein complexes during fermentation. Oxygen radical absorbance capacity (ORAC) increased significantly during storage in before-fermentation variants, suggesting progressive release of bound phenolics through starter culture-mediated proteolysis. Decaffeinated lyophilizate added before fermentation produced the firmest yogurt gel, an effect potentially attributable to polyphenol-casein interactions and possible caffeine-mediated modification of starter culture activity. Addition timing rather than coffee type was the primary determinant of surface optical properties. The majority of bioactive compound profiles and physicochemical parameters showed no systematic changes during the 20-d storage period, although significant storage-related changes were observed for selected antioxidant activity indices, textural parameters, surface gloss, and diterpene content in specific treatment groups. These findings indicate that coffee lyophilizate is a promising functional ingredient for yogurt enrichment, with the timing of addition being a critical process parameter that influences bioactive compound availability, antioxidant functionality, and textural quality.

papers.title: Functional characterization and safety assessment of tea-derived Aspergillus sydowii, a core microbe capable of concurrent theabrownins production and caffeine degradation.
papers.abstractText: The distinct quality of dark tea is predominantly formed in pile fermentation by a consortium of functional microbes, yet their specific roles remain poorly understood. In this study, Aspergillus sydowii was isolated from dark tea, and thoroughly investigated for its functional characteristics and potential safety risk. A. sydowii-driving fermentation reduced the fresh, bitter, astringent taste, while imparting stale, thick, and mellow in final fermented tea. Intriguingly, A. sydowii demonstrates remarkable capacity for producing theabrownins and degrading caffeine, with theabrownins up to 157.77 g/kg and caffeine low to 4.81 g/kg. 51 differential metabolites were identified, with hydrolysis/polymerization of catechins, degradation of caffeine, deglycosylation of flavonoid glycosides, and N-ethyl-2-pyrrolidinone substitution of flavan-3-ols. Under the tested 9-day fermentation conditions, no detectable levels of mycotoxins were found in A. sydowii-fermented tea. This work provides a benchmark for the safe application of A. sydowii in the industrial production of high-theabrownins low-caffeine dark tea.

papers.title: Fate and Antioxidant Activity of Matcha Catechins during Lactic Acid Bacteria Fermentation
papers.abstractText: Abstract    Matcha is widely applied in fermented foods because of its abundant catechins, dietary fiber and health effects, but the fate of catechins during lactic acid bacteria (LAB) fermentation and its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Hence, the effects of LAB (Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus) fermentation on the catechins release from matcha, and its relationship with antioxidant capacity were investigated. The results showed that aqueous extraction yielded 43% free catechins, whereas 70% methanol recovered nearly 90%. LAB fermentation increased the concentrations of TPC, catechin, CG, GC, GCG, EGC, EGCG, gallic acid, and caffeine. Lactose co-fermentation dramatically elevated catechin release (230.8%) and gallic acid (127.4%) while reducing the proportion of total epicatechin-type catechins. Mechanistically, LAB fermentation promotes EGCG and ECG conversion into EGC, catechin, and gallic acid via multiple pathways. Antioxidant assays revealed that DPPH, •OH, and •O2− scavenging capacities and total reducing power correlated positively with the epicatechin-type catechins concentrations, especially EGCG and EGC. Overall, matcha catechins release during LAB fermentation is co-regulated by acidochemical desorption, dietary fiber degradation, and enzymatic bioconversion. Matcha dosage, lactose availability, and strain metabolic activity collectively determine the final catechins profile, release degree, and antioxidant performance. These findings provide a theoretical basis and practical guidance for fermented matcha products.

papers.title: Coffee consumption and chronic kidney disease.
papers.abstractText: Coffee is one of the most widely consumed beverages globally. Caffeine has been linked to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antifibrotic, and anticancer effects. However, the relationship between caffeine consumption and the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD) has yielded conflicting findings. Research on the health effects of caffeine relies mainly on exploratory observational studies, which may be affected by biases such as residual confounding. Variations in behaviour, health status, intake, and metabolism also influence outcomes. A comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms and population-specific factors mediating the impact of caffeine on kidney health is essential. In this article, we describe the metabolism and mechanism of action of caffeine, as well as its potential adverse effects. We synthesize current evidence and clarify the complex relationship between caffeine, CKD, and cardiovascular disease. Current evidence suggests that moderate caffeine intake is probably safe in CKD and may be potentially beneficial. Stronger evidence is needed before robust recommendations can be made for clinical practice.
